authority.statement: Go/no-go on which organisation is attacked sits with the licensee, not with the core. The core holds a near-monopoly over admission to the programme, the build pipeline, the leak site, the victim-negotiation portal, the price floor and the payment split, and it can expel a licensee after the fact; it does not select victims and in the dominant brands does not see a victim before deployment. Authority is therefore split by decision type — centralized over strategy, pricing and rails, delegated over targeting — which is why a single decisionCentralization scalar is weakly identified.
authority.basis: CISA, FBI, MS-ISAC and six partner agencies, Advisory AA23-165A, 'Understanding Ransomware Threat Actors: LockBit', 14 June 2023, attributes wide TTP variance directly to the 'large number of unconnected affiliates in the operation'. The 7 May 2025 dump of a LockBit affiliate-panel database (records 18 Dec 2024 - 29 Apr 2025) shows the core owning build generation, victim records, negotiation chat and a ~20% cut, plus per-affiliate registration fees — Trellix Advanced Research Center, 'Inside LockBit's Admin Panel Leak' (2025); TRM Labs, 'LockBit Leak Provides Insight into Ransomware-as-a-Service Enterprise' (2025). Principal counter-evidence for a more hierarchical reading: Paternoster, Nazzari, Jofre and Uberti, 'Inside the Leak: Exploring the Structure of the Conti Ransomware Group', Global Crime 26(2), 2025, 148-171, find a firm-like core with identifiable leadership in the leaked Conti corpus (n=168,740). Confidence held at medium because the split is read off two brands' internal data and Chainalysis (2026 Crypto Crime Report) counts ~85 active extortion brands, most of which have never been observed from the inside.

steps.office: The core programme's affiliate-recruitment function, operating through closed Russian-language crime forums
steps.gate: Rejects applicants who cannot produce forum tenure, a positive reputation and a deposit. The filter is against researchers and law-enforcement infiltration, not against target choice — nothing at this stage constrains who a licensee will later attack. The threshold has risen since 2024 without the mechanism changing shape.
steps.basis: RAMP's published registration conditions on reopening, 13 Aug 2021, required an existing XSS or Exploit.in account with at least two months of history and positive reputation plus a registration fee reported at ~$500 (CloudSEK, 'The Rise and Fall of RAMP: Inside the Forum Where Ransomware Was Always Welcome', 2025; SOCRadar, 'Dark Web Forum: RAMP'). Recorded Future Insikt Group, 'Dark Covenant 3.0: Controlled Impunity and Russia's Cybercriminals' (2025), reports programme owners becoming more selective after Operation Endgame with the core mechanics intact and the entry threshold rising. Weakened by venue churn rather than by mechanism change: XSS.is was taken down in July 2025 and RAMP was seized by US authorities on 28 Jan 2026 (Rapid7, 'The Post-RAMP Era', 2026). All of this is industry reporting on closed forums, not a primary document.

steps.office: The licensee's own operator team, purchasing from the third-party initial-access-broker market rather than developing access in-house
steps.gate: Price and quality of the access on offer, not the identity of the organisation behind it. This stage is where the actor's opportunism is manufactured: the victim set for a given week is largely whatever the access market happened to be selling, which is the mechanism behind the profile's low rationalityPrecision.
steps.basis: Chainalysis, 2026 Crypto Crime Report (ransomware section), puts initial-access-broker on-chain inflows at ~$14M for 2025 with advertised access prices falling from ~$1,427 (Q1 2023) to $439 (Q1 2026). Mandiant, M-Trends 2026, reports a median initial-access-to-ransomware-affiliate handoff of 22 seconds in 2025, down from over eight hours in 2022 — a measure of market liquidity, not of the actor's planning horizon, and the profile's timeHorizon basis flags that misreading explicitly. Medium rather than high because neither source establishes what share of any single brand's victims arrive through purchased access as against self-developed intrusion.

steps.office: The core's affiliate panel, backed by a salaried in-house development function
steps.gate: Issues a target-specific build and key pair, and hard-codes the one filter this actor actually enforces before execution — an abort on shelter-jurisdiction system indicators. Nothing at this stage inspects the victim's sector, size or criticality.
steps.basis: Mandiant, 'Shining a Light on DARKSIDE Ransomware Operations' (2021), documents execution gated on a system-locale and keyboard-layout check that aborts on CIS systems — a targeting rule implemented in code rather than in policy, and the only one that survived when a major brand voided all other exclusions in Dec 2023. The leaked LockBit panel shows per-victim build generation for LockBit Black 4.0 and Green 4.0 across Windows, Linux and ESXi (Trellix, 2025). The development function is salaried rather than commission-based: US Department of Justice, 'United States Charges Dual Russian and Israeli National as Developer of LockBit Ransomware Group', press release and criminal complaint (D.N.J.), 20 Dec 2024, alleges ~$10,000 per month in cryptocurrency totalling more than $230,000 from June 2022 to February 2024 for malware development and consulting. Medium because the DOJ document is a charging allegation and the locale-check evidence is from one brand's tooling generalised across the class.

steps.office: The licensee's operator team, with tooling and staging support drawn from the core's shared services
steps.gate: Aborts or pivots where the environment can restore itself. Backup posture, not sector and not expected harm, is the decisive variable — the negotiation literature finds it the dominant determinant of whether a victim pays at all. Exfiltration completes here because the retained copy is the leverage that survives a successful restore.
steps.basis: Meurs, Cartwright, Cartwright, Houba and Woods, 'The Ransomware Pricing Paradox: An Empirical Study of the Six Stages of Ransomware Negotiations', Tinbergen Institute Discussion Paper TI 2025-052/VII (rev. Oct 2025), covering 481 police-reported incidents and 237 negotiation transcripts across 23 groups, finds backup status the dominant determinant of payment. Secureworks, State of the Threat (2023), reports median ransomware dwell time just under 24 hours with deployment inside five hours in just over 10% of cases. The abort behaviour is inferred from payment-determinant data rather than observed as an explicit decision in any recovered internal record, which caps confidence here.

steps.office: The licensee, acting unilaterally; core-level victim approval exists only as declared policy
steps.gate: What is actually decided here is timing — off-hours, holidays, fiscal events — not eligibility. The one brand that announced a core-level pre-encryption approval gate announced it after the incident that prompted it and exited three days later, so the gate has never been observed operating on a live target.
steps.basis: DarkSide's 'About the latest news' posting, c. 10 May 2021: 'From today we introduce moderation and check each company that our partners want to encrypt to avoid social consequences in the future', followed by its 13 May 2021 announcement of lost infrastructure and brand exit — the actor's own declaratory text, reported contemporaneously (Vice/Motherboard, 10 May 2021; Axios, 14 May 2021), used for nothing but what it said. The profile's declaredVsObserved section records this as post-hoc announcement rather than observed pre-emptive avoidance. Timing selection: Cl0p's MOVEit mass exploitation was launched over the US Memorial Day weekend beginning 27 May 2023 (Kroll, 'Clop Ransomware: MOVEit Transfer Vulnerability CVE-2023-34362', June 2023).

steps.office: The core's victim-portal negotiation desk, working to a core-set floor price and delegated discount authority
steps.gate: Sets the opening demand against estimated victim revenue and bounds how far a licensee may discount. This gate stops nothing on harm grounds; what it stops is a licensee settling below the floor or off-platform.
steps.basis: Meurs et al. (TI 2025-052/VII, 2025) document a six-stage negotiation with revenue-scaled dynamic pricing and a high-demand-then-large-discount structure as standard practice rather than as failure. Sophos, The State of Ransomware 2025, finds 53% of payers paid below the initial demand, payers averaged 85% of it, and 71% of reductions were obtained through negotiation. The leaked LockBit panel carried the negotiation chat interface alongside victim records and the core's cut (Trellix, 2025). The existence of an enforced floor is inferred from the discount distribution and the panel's controls; no recovered pricing policy document states one, so this is the weakest-evidenced gate in the chain.

steps.office: The core's payment and publicity function, with laundering and hosting outsourced to third-party bulletproof providers
steps.gate: The only stage at which an external legal fact can stop the transaction: a sanctions designation touching the actor or its rail converts payment into an illegal act for the victim and removes the settlement from the choice set entirely. Note the inversion one major brand used — the licensee receives the payment first and remits the core's cut — which is a labour-market trust instrument, not a control.
steps.basis: CISA/FBI AA23-165A, 14 June 2023, records affiliates being paid before the core, an inversion of normal RaaS practice. US Treasury/OFAC designations of bulletproof-hosting providers Zservers (Feb 2025), Aeza Group (July 2025) and Media Land (Nov 2025) evidence the outsourced hosting and laundering layer and the enforcement pivot toward it. Trellix (2025) observes a ~20% core cut in the leaked panel, roughly $456,000 on ~$2.3M over five months. Chainalysis (2026) reports the payment rate at ~28%, an apparent all-time low, against a 50% rise in claimed attacks — most settlements now fail at this stage rather than earlier ones.

tempo.statement: Two clocks run, and they are commonly confused. The intrusion-to-encryption clock is hours to days and compressing; the negotiation clock is days to weeks and is the one the core actually manages. No stage in the chain requires an authorisation cycle longer than a chat message, so against this actor the defender's decision loop is usually the slower one — which is a statement about the absence of internal veto points, not about the actor's patience.
tempo.basis: Secureworks, State of the Threat (2023): median dwell just under 24 hours, deployment inside five hours in just over 10% of cases. Mandiant, M-Trends 2026: median initial-access-to-affiliate handoff of 22 seconds in 2025, while overall median dwell time rose to 14 days in the same edition — the two figures measure different things (access-market liquidity versus time resident in the network) and quoting the 22-second figure as a planning horizon is the specific error the profile's timeHorizon basis was rewritten to prevent. Negotiation duration: Meurs et al. (TI 2025-052/VII, 2025) and University of Twente et al., 'Engaging with cybercriminals: phases and influence strategies in ransomware negotiations', Computers in Human Behavior (2026), 41 authentic negotiation logs.

preconditions.statement: The shelter-jurisdiction check must pass. This is enforced in the build rather than in policy, which is why it survives enforcement pressure that voids every declared rule.
preconditions.basis: Mandiant (2021) documents the locale/keyboard-layout abort on CIS systems. It was the sole exclusion retained when a major brand publicly voided all others on 19-20 Dec 2023. Recorded Future Insikt Group, Dark Covenant 3.0 (2025), characterises the shelter as externally granted, selective, managed and revocable — which makes this precondition, uniquely among the four, something an intervention could in principle remove. Medium: the shelter relationship is inferred from arrest geography and prosecution patterns, not from any document either party has published.

preconditions.statement: Exfiltration must complete before encryption, because the retained copy is the only leverage that survives a successful restore.
preconditions.basis: Meurs et al. (TI 2025-052/VII, 2025) find backup status the dominant determinant of payment, which is what makes the exfiltrated copy load-bearing rather than supplementary. US government #StopRansomware victim guidance states payment does not guarantee deletion — the same fact from the other side, and the basis of the profile's no-verifiable-data-deletion item.

preconditions.statement: The victim must be revenue-estimable, because the demand is scaled to ability to pay rather than to the cost of the harm inflicted.
preconditions.basis: Meurs et al. (2025) document revenue-scaled dynamic pricing across 237 negotiation transcripts. Theoretical framing in Cartwright, Hernandez-Castro and Stepanova, 'To pay or not: game theoretic models of ransomware', Journal of Cybersecurity 5(1), 2019, on uniform pricing versus price discrimination versus bargaining. Chainalysis (2026) reports median payment up 368% to ~$59.5K alongside the record-low payment rate — the profile flags that this is at least partly a composition effect as smaller victims stop paying, not proof of harsher pricing.

preconditions.statement: A payment rail must exist that no sanctions designation has closed. This is an instrumental sensitivity to the victim's legal environment, not a legitimacy constraint, and it binds at settlement rather than at target selection.
preconditions.basis: OFAC designations of the brand and of hosting/laundering providers (Zservers Feb 2025; Aeza July 2025; Media Land Nov 2025) operate by converting payment into a legal act for the victim rather than by raising the actor's costs. Institute for Security and Technology, Ransomware Task Force, 'Combating Ransomware' (2021) and 'The RTF at 5 Years' (2026), frame the business model rather than the operators as the disruption target. The profile's legitimacyWeight basis insists this sensitivity be booked to cost and payment-channel variables, never to legitimacy.

afterAction.statement: There is no after-action review in an institutional sense. The institution dissolves, rebrands, and carries personnel, tooling and forum reputation into the successor; learning is embodied in code (locale guards, panel hardening, decentralised comms) and in market reputation rather than in doctrine. The practical consequence for a modeller is that a lesson learned by one brand is not reliably held by the next, and that disruption resets tradecraft far less than it resets branding.
afterAction.basis: Europol, IOCTA 2025 ('Steal, Deal and Repeat'), records 120+ active brands with affiliates and administrators operating across several of them simultaneously. Conti's wind-down on c. 19 May 2022 dispersed into successor brands rather than ending the operation (BleepingComputer, 19-21 May 2022; Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, 'The rise and fall of the Conti ransomware group', 2023). Recorded Future, Dark Covenant 3.0 (2025), reports post-disruption tightening of affiliate vetting and a shift to decentralised communication platforms — the clearest observed instance of the ecosystem, rather than any single firm, updating. Medium: 'the ecosystem learns' is an aggregate claim assembled from brand-level observations, and no source demonstrates a within-brand review process.

declaredEnds.statement: Revenue, stated as the entire objective, with an explicit disclaimer of political ends.
declaredEnds.basis: DarkSide's 'About the latest news' posting, c. 10 May 2021: 'We are apolitical, we do not participate in geopolitics, do not need to tie us with a defined government and look for our motives. Our goal is to make money, and not creating problems for society.' Contemporaneous reporting (Vice/Motherboard, 10 May 2021), used only as the actor's own declaratory text. Confidence is medium and not high for a reason the profile states plainly: this actor class lies in public postings, and the same statement's promise of target moderation was never observed to operate before the brand exited three days later.

declaredEnds.statement: Share of the licensee labour market, pursued explicitly and openly through publicity — the leak site is a recruitment instrument as much as a coercion instrument.
declaredEnds.basis: CISA/FBI AA23-165A, 14 June 2023, lists publicity-generating stunts among the means used to attract affiliates, including the frequently miscited $1M bounty offer, which the advisory categorises as a recruitment stunt rather than as evidence of anti-doxxing resolve. The leaked LockBit panel shows per-affiliate registration fees and accounting consistent with a programme sold to operators, not only run by them (Trellix, 2025). Affiliates were paid before the core, an inversion of normal practice that only makes sense as a labour-market reputation instrument (AA23-165A).

declaredEnds.statement: Continuity of the brand through law-enforcement disruption, declared as an objective in its own right and pursued at a loss.
declaredEnds.basis: LockBit posted an account of the Operation Cronos breach and its rebuild plan within five days of the 19 Feb 2024 seizure (BankInfoSecurity, Feb 2024; Trend Micro, 'Unveiling the Fallout: Operation Cronos' Impact on LockBit', Apr 2024), and the brand relaunched again as LockBit 5.0 in Sept 2025 with 15+ distinct victims identified in Q3 2025 (Check Point Research, Q3 2025). This is the one declared end the record shows being funded out of degraded revenue rather than out of profit, and it is the main tension with the profile's low ownCostTolerance.

selfImage.statement: Presents itself as a firm — a licensing business with a product, a support desk, a pricing policy and staff — rather than as a conspiracy or a political actor. Unusually for self-description, the internal record corroborates it: recovered material shows salaried employees, functional divisions and performance management rather than a loose crew.
selfImage.basis: The leaked Conti corpus shows salaried staff, an HR function, recruitment, and functional divisions; characterised by Check Point Research, 'Leaks of Conti Ransomware Group Paint Picture of a Surprisingly Normal Tech Start-Up... Sort Of' (Mar 2022), and analysed formally by Paternoster, Nazzari, Jofre and Uberti, Global Crime 26(2), 2025, 148-171, which finds a hierarchical, firm-like structure with discernible leadership and clear division of labour (n=168,740 messages; the first public tranche was ~60,000). Corroborating primary allegation: US DOJ, 20 Dec 2024, alleges a fixed ~$10,000/month salary for a core developer over 20 months — employment, not a share of proceeds. Medium: both windows are into brands that were compromised, and compromised brands may not be representative of the ~85 currently active.

threatModel.statement: Legal identification of its principals, and their presence in an extradition-cooperative jurisdiction. Infrastructure seizure is treated as a recoverable operating cost; identification is treated as the thing that cannot be undone.
threatModel.basis: Operation Cronos seized 34 servers, the affiliate panel, cryptocurrency addresses and 1,000+ decryption keys on 19 Feb 2024 (UK National Crime Agency, 20 Feb 2024) and the brand was operating again within five days (Trend Micro, Apr 2024). The May 2024 NCA/OFAC/AFP identification and designation of the brand's lead degraded it further, yet it relaunched in Sept 2025 (Check Point, Q3 2025). Which of the two did the greater damage is contested rather than settled: Analyst1, 'LockBit Takedown and Operation Cronos' (2024) and 'Ransomware Diaries Volume 5' (2024-25), attributes the licensee exodus and the collapse in affiliate access pricing to the seizure operation itself. The profile treats this as its least defensible parameter for exactly this reason.

threatModel.statement: Insiders and infiltrators — the disclosure risk it can neither price nor insure against, and the reason the vetting gate exists at all.
threatModel.basis: The Feb-Mar 2022 leak of Conti's internal chats by an apparent insider objecting to the group's pro-Kremlin statement (TechCrunch, 28 Feb 2022; The Record, Mar 2022). The 7 May 2025 defacement of a LockBit panel and publication of its database dump by an unidentified actor (Trellix, 2025). Recorded Future, Dark Covenant 3.0 (2025), reports eroding trust inside the underground, with affiliates complaining of scams, impersonation and selective enforcement. Medium: the 2025 panel hacker's motive and identity remain unknown, so it evidences the exposure rather than the source of it.

threatModel.statement: Revocation of the shelter it operates under — a conditional, externally granted permission rather than a possession, and the only threat on this list the actor cannot mitigate through tradecraft.
threatModel.basis: Recorded Future Insikt Group, Dark Covenant 3.0: Controlled Impunity and Russia's Cybercriminals (events through Sept 2025), describes a shift from passive tolerance to selective, managed and revocable enforcement. Confidence is capped at low-to-medium: the relationship is inferred from arrest and prosecution patterns by a commercial intelligence vendor, no primary document from either side exists, and the profile's uncertainty section names this as the single most behaviourally consequential thing its schema cannot currently represent.

threatModel.statement: Victims who can restore without paying, together with the professionalised incident-response, negotiation and insurance apparatus around them — a commercial threat to the revenue model rather than a threat to the operators.
threatModel.basis: Meurs et al. (2025) find backup status the dominant determinant of payment across 481 incidents. Chainalysis (2026) reports payments falling to $820M in 2025, down 8% year on year and 35% from 2023's $1.25B, with the payment rate at ~28% against a 50% rise in claimed attacks — the actor is attacking more and collecting less. Sophos (2025) finds 71% of ransom reductions were obtained through negotiation, i.e. by a professionalised counterparty.

adversaryModel.statement: Models the victim as a rational payer whose decision turns on restorability and disclosure exposure rather than on principle, and expects to negotiate — a high opening demand followed by a large discount is the designed path, not a failure. It models law enforcement as able to take infrastructure and money but not persons inside the shelter, which is why it treats a takedown as an operating cost and does not retaliate against it. Both models are partly wrong, and the same way: it consistently underestimates the probability that a victim it selected commercially triggers a state-level response.
adversaryModel.basis: Negotiation expectations: Sophos, State of Ransomware 2025 (payers averaged 85% of the initial demand; 53% paid below ask, 29% at ask, 18% above; 71% of reductions via negotiation) and Meurs et al. (2025) on the six-stage structure. Law-enforcement model: the observed response to Operation Cronos was reconstitution, not reprisal (NCA, Feb 2024; Trend Micro, Apr 2024). The overconfidence finding rests on two episodes — Colonial Pipeline (May 2021) and Kaseya (July 2021) — which is thin evidence for a general claim, and is the reason the profile encodes escalationControlBelief as a belief the record shows to be overconfident rather than as demonstrated capability.

declaredIdeology.statement: The only programmatic text this actor class issues about itself is an affiliate rules-of-engagement posting: an explicitly apolitical profit doctrine plus a target-exclusion list. Both limbs are unreliable in specific, checkable ways. The exclusions are drafted to preserve the revenue-bearing limb — one brand's published rule prohibited encrypting medical institutions 'where attacks could lead to death' while expressly permitting theft of their data — and another brand voided every exclusion but the shelter jurisdiction within hours of a law-enforcement seizure. There is no political, territorial or normative programme, and the profile's strongest negative finding is that this actor has no ideological redline to protect.
declaredIdeology.basis: DarkSide's 'About the latest news' posting, c. 10 May 2021 (apolitical, profit-motivated, announcing target moderation). LockBit's published affiliate rules prohibiting encryption of medical institutions while permitting data theft from them, reported in the coverage of its 31 Dec 2022 SickKids reversal (BleepingComputer, 1 Jan 2023; CSO Online, Jan 2023). ALPHV/BlackCat's 19-20 Dec 2023 rules posting: 'we are introducing new rules, or rather removing ALL the rules except one, you can not touch the CIS, you can now block hospitals, nuclear power plants, anything and anywhere' (contemporaneous reporting, BleepingComputer; Barracuda Networks blog, Mar 2024); the underlying disruption is documented in CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-353A, '#StopRansomware: ALPHV Blackcat' (Dec 2023 update). Confidence is low and should stay low: these are self-published postings by an actor class that lies in public, and the profile's declaredVsObserved section records that observed targeting contradicts every exclusion in them.

history.episode: Three US federal agencies issued an unprecedented joint advisory warning of an 'increased and imminent cybercrime threat' to US hospitals, naming Ryuk and Conti, while the operators were mid-campaign against the healthcare sector during the COVID-19 pandemic.
history.choice: Acted, and kept acting. The operators pressed a campaign against hospitals at the point of maximum leverage and maximum political heat, and did not stand down when three federal agencies named them in public.
history.lesson: Acted, and absorbed public attribution without changing behaviour. The clearest observed evidence that harm to noncombatants is not a constraint on this institution but a source of coercive leverage, and that being named by a government is not by itself a cost it prices. It is the observed-conduct anchor for counterpartHarmRestraint at 0.15, against declared exclusions that would have implied roughly 0.45.
history.basis: CISA, FBI and HHS, Joint Cybersecurity Advisory AA20-302A, 'Ransomware Activity Targeting the Healthcare and Public Health Sector', 28 Oct 2020, updated 29 Oct 2020 to add Conti, TrickBot and BazarLoader. Consequence anchor rather than preference measure: McGlave, Neprash and Nikpay, 'Hacked to Pieces? The Effects of Ransomware Attacks on Hospitals and Patients', American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 18(1), 2026, 256-81, find in-hospital mortality rises 34-38% for patients already admitted when an attack begins. Medium rather than high because the continuation is the aggregate of many licensees' separate choices, not a recorded institutional decision to persist.

history.episode: Eleven days after the Colonial Pipeline attack triggered a US fuel-supply emergency and direct presidential comment, DarkSide announced it had lost its infrastructure and funds and wound the brand down. Three days earlier it had posted that it was apolitical, that its goal was 'to make money, and not creating problems for society', and that from that day it would check each company its partners wanted to encrypt.
history.choice: Withdrew. It abandoned the brand rather than carry state-level attention, and issued a target-vetting policy only after the incident that prompted it.
history.lesson: Held nothing and dissolved. The institution absorbs almost no enforcement cost: it exits and re-forms rather than paying to keep a brand alive. It also fixes the ceiling on escalation control — a licensee's ordinary commercial target selection produced a national-emergency response the core neither predicted nor wanted, which is why escalationControlBelief encodes a belief rather than a demonstrated capability. The apolitical statement is a legitimacy claim addressed to the labour market and the shelter, not a constraint that operated before the attack.
history.basis: DarkSide's 'About the latest news' posting, c. 10 May 2021, and its 13 May 2021 shutdown announcement, both as reported contemporaneously (Vice/Motherboard, 10 May 2021; Axios, 14 May 2021) — journalism, used only for the actor's own declaratory text. Mandiant, 'Shining a Light on DARKSIDE Ransomware Operations' (2021), for the affiliate rules of engagement and the CIS locale check. The profile's declaredVsObserved section records the vetting promise as a post-hoc announcement of future vetting followed by brand exit, not as evidence of pre-emptive target avoidance, and this episode should not be cited as restraint.

history.episode: Conti declared 'full support of the Russian government' on 25 Feb 2022 and threatened critical-infrastructure reprisals against anyone attacking Russia; an apparent insider objecting to that statement leaked the group's internal chats within days; the operation wound down around 19 May 2022 and dispersed into successor brands.
history.choice: Acted politically once, then absorbed a catastrophic internal disclosure and dissolved rather than defend the brand.
history.lesson: Acted, then dissolved. The single episode in the record where this actor class took a political side, and it was punished from inside its own organisation — which is why the profile carries no ideological redline and why any values-based hard constraint on this actor would be an artifact. The wind-down was multi-causal (a costly campaign against one government, sanctions converting payment into a legal act, and the leak), so it is not clean evidence that the disclosure alone ended the brand. The same corpus is simultaneously the strongest evidence that the core is a hierarchical firm rather than a loose network, and is the principal counter-evidence against a low decisionCentralization value.
history.basis: Conti's 25 Feb 2022 posting and the ContiLeaks disclosure beginning 27-28 Feb 2022 (TechCrunch, 28 Feb 2022; The Record, Mar 2022; Check Point Research, Mar 2022, on the first tranche of ~60,094 messages). Wind-down reported 19-21 May 2022 (BleepingComputer; The Hacker News). Structure findings on the full corpus (n=168,740): Paternoster, Nazzari, Jofre and Uberti, Global Crime 26(2), 2025, 148-171, doi:10.1080/17440572.2025.2473350, and a companion 2025 Global Crime study on organisational units and communication patterns, doi:10.1080/17440572.2025.2534387 (paywalled; abstract only).

history.episode: Thirteen days after a licensee encrypted the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, the LockBit core publicly apologised on its leak site, published a free decryptor, and stated that the licensee had violated its rules and had been expelled from the affiliate programme. The hospital did not pay and did not use the decryptor.
history.choice: Refused, retroactively. It forfeited the revenue on a live extortion and expelled the licensee — the only sanction the core actually holds.
history.lesson: Held — but only after the fact, and only on the limb of the rule that does not bear revenue. The published rule prohibited encrypting medical institutions where the attack could cause death while expressly permitting theft of their data, so the enforcement action protected standing in the licensee labour market at close to the minimum commercial cost. It is genuine restraint and it is narrow: the same brand appears in a government advisory as a healthcare attacker six months later. The episode also locates authority precisely — the core can expel a licensee after the fact and cannot prevent the attack — which is the split the profile's decisionCentralization note describes.
history.basis: LockBit's leak-site posting of 31 Dec 2022 and the free decryptor, reported contemporaneously (BleepingComputer, 1 Jan 2023; CSO Online, Jan 2023; Healthcare IT News, Jan 2023; Infosecurity Magazine). The hospital's confirmation that it neither paid nor used the decryptor (CBC News, Jan 2023). The encrypt-versus-exfiltrate carve-out in the published rules appears in the same coverage. Continued sector targeting: CISA/FBI AA23-165A, 14 June 2023, lists healthcare among sectors attacked by LockBit affiliates. Medium: the apology is the actor's own declaratory text and the motive attributed to it is inferred, not documented.

history.episode: Cl0p claimed mass exploitation of a MOVEit Transfer zero-day (CVE-2023-34362) it had been testing since at least July 2021, launched over the US Memorial Day weekend beginning 27 May 2023; days later it posted that government, city and police victims need 'not worry, we erased all your data'.
history.choice: Acted at scale on a capability held unspent for roughly two years, and simultaneously declined to extort one class of victim.
history.lesson: Held, then acted. Contradicts a purely short-horizon reading of this actor: the capability was held for about two years and released only once the tooling supported mass simultaneous collection, which is why timeHorizon is encoded at 0.3 rather than at the near-zero the 22-second handoff figure would suggest. The declared carve-out for government and police victims is not restraint about harm — it is avoidance of the single response class the actor cannot absorb, and it was never verified; federal agencies were confirmed among the compromised. Brand attribution was sought loudly at the same moment legal exposure was minimised, which is exactly the split construct attributionAversion encodes.
history.basis: Kroll, 'Clop Ransomware: MOVEit Transfer Vulnerability CVE-2023-34362' (June 2023), dates manual exploitation testing to July 2021, automated multi-organisation probing from April 2022, scaled activity from 15 May 2023, and mass exploitation from 27 May 2023. CISA and FBI, Advisory AA23-158A, '#StopRansomware: CL0P Ransomware Gang Exploits CVE-2023-34362 MOVEit Vulnerability', 7 June 2023. The 'we erased all your data' text is the actor's own leak-site posting, reported contemporaneously (The Record, 6 June 2023). Medium: the deletion claim is unverifiable and should be read as declaratory, and the two-year hold is Kroll's forensic inference from command similarity rather than a recovered decision record.

history.episode: ALPHV/BlackCat filed a whistleblower complaint with the US Securities and Exchange Commission against its own victim, MeridianLink, for failing to disclose the breach, published a screenshot of the complaint under the headline 'MeridianLink fails to file with the SEC ...so we do it for them', and attached a 24-hour deadline.
history.choice: Escalated into the victim's regulatory environment rather than into further technical harm.
history.lesson: Escalated, through law rather than through damage. This is what the profile means by zero normative legitimacy weight combined with high instrumental sensitivity to the victim's legal environment: the actor invokes a regulator whose jurisdiction it is itself a fugitive from, because the victim's disclosure exposure is a cheaper lever than more encryption. It also shows the escalation-control belief is overconfident in a checkable way — the disclosure rule the complaint relied on had not yet reached its compliance date, so the lever the actor believed it was pulling did not exist.
history.basis: ALPHV's leak-site posting and published complaint screenshot, reported 15-16 Nov 2023 (BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek; The Record, which also reported MeridianLink's confirmation of the incident). The SEC's cybersecurity disclosure requirement (Form 8-K Item 1.05, adopted July 2023) had a compliance date of 18 Dec 2023 for most registrants and later for smaller reporting companies — after the complaint was filed. Medium: the event and the timing gap are well documented; the inference about what the actor believed is exactly that, an inference.

history.episode: Hours after an FBI-led operation seized its leak site and distributed decryption keys, ALPHV/BlackCat re-established infrastructure and posted new rules: 'we are introducing new rules, or rather removing ALL the rules except one, you can not touch the CIS, you can now block hospitals, nuclear power plants, anything and anywhere'.
history.choice: Escalated under a loss frame — voided every declared targeting limit except the shelter jurisdiction and widened what its licensees were permitted to attack.
history.lesson: Escalated. Under enforcement pressure the institution accepts risk it otherwise avoids, and the risk it spends is other people's safety rather than its own exposure — the one rule retained was the one protecting its principals. It also identifies where the binding constraint actually sits: the asset worth voiding every remaining rule for is the licensee labour base, because the core cannot generate victims without it, which is the behavioural content of proxyPreference at 0.85. The episode is the primary evidence for lossFrameRiskAcceptance at 0.65.
history.basis: ALPHV's 19-20 Dec 2023 rules posting, reported contemporaneously (BleepingComputer; Barracuda Networks blog, Mar 2024) — declaratory text from an actor class that lies in public, therefore corroborative only. The underlying disruption is documented in CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-353A, '#StopRansomware: ALPHV Blackcat' (Dec 2023 update), and in the US DOJ/FBI announcement of 19 Dec 2023. The consequence is recorded in the same advisory's 27 Feb 2024 update, which states that since mid-December 2023, of the nearly 70 leaked victims, healthcare was the most commonly victimised sector, 'likely in response to the ALPHV Blackcat administrator's post encouraging its affiliates to target hospitals after operational action against the group and its infrastructure in early December 2023'.

history.episode: After a licensee's attack on Change Healthcare produced an apparent ~$22M payment, the ALPHV core took the entire payment, posted a fake law-enforcement seizure banner on its own site, and exited — defrauding the licensee, which still held the exfiltrated data and said so publicly.
history.choice: Defected against its own surrogate, taking a one-time cash-out over the continuing enterprise.
history.lesson: Acted, at the expense of the enterprise. Bounds the time horizon from above: offered a large enough single payment, the core will liquidate its own brand and its own labour relationships rather than compound them, which is the main evidence against reading timeHorizon up toward the multi-year brand persistence the same actor otherwise displays. It locates the payment rail firmly with the core — the licensee could not collect around it. And it is the concrete demonstration that a settlement cannot bind whoever physically holds the data, which is why the no-verifiable-data-deletion item is an inability to commit rather than a refusal.
history.basis: B. Krebs, 'BlackCat Ransomware Group Implodes After Apparent $22M Ransom Payment by Change Healthcare', Krebs on Security, 5 Mar 2024, reporting the affiliate's own account posted to a Russian-language crime forum; corroborated by contemporaneous coverage (S-RM, Cyber Intelligence Briefing, 12 Mar 2024; HIPAA Journal, Mar 2024). Medium and not higher: the affiliate's account is self-interested, and the payment was not confirmed by the victim at the time of the episode.

history.episode: Operation Cronos seized 34 servers, the affiliate panel, cryptocurrency addresses and over 1,000 decryption keys from LockBit. The brand re-established a leak site within five days, continued operating through the May 2024 identification and designation of its lead, and relaunched again as LockBit 5.0 in September 2025.
history.choice: Absorbed the loss and rebuilt. It did not retaliate against law enforcement and it did not alter its jurisdiction of residence.
history.lesson: Absorbed cost — the standing exception to this actor's otherwise low cost tolerance, and the episode that marks where the real commitment sits. Brand and infrastructure are replaceable and were replaced; what was never traded at any price was the principals' legal identity or their presence in a non-extraditing jurisdiction, which is the principal-liberty-preservation redline. Against a state adversary it shows no reciprocity whatsoever: no reprisal, only reconstitution, which is why the profile carries no compels_response redline and treats any modelled tit-for-tat here as an artifact. The contested part matters: Analyst1 attributes the licensee exodus and the collapse in affiliate access pricing (~$10,000 to ~$700) to the seizure itself rather than to the later public identification, so 'naming the lead was decisive' is not established.
history.basis: UK National Crime Agency, 'The NCA announces the disruption of LockBit with Operation Cronos', 20 Feb 2024. Trend Micro, 'Unveiling the Fallout: Operation Cronos' Impact on LockBit Following Landmark Disruption', Apr 2024; five-day relaunch reported contemporaneously (BankInfoSecurity; Dark Reading, Feb 2024). May 2024 NCA/OFAC/AFP designation of the brand's lead. Relaunch and Q3 2025 victim count: Check Point Research, 'LockBit 5.0: Ransomware Gang Returns in Force' (2025). Contested causal attribution: Analyst1, 'LockBit Takedown & Operation Cronos: A Long-Awaited PsyOps Against Ransomware' (2024) and 'Ransomware Diaries Volume 5' (2024-25).
